findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
findings.body: The lookup compares the raw submitted email with the raw stored email. Email local/domain casing is commonly accepted by this application (and the domain restriction check is case-insensitive), so a blocked entry such as `spam@example.com` will not match a signup submitted as `Spam@Example.com` on the normal case-sensitive varchar comparison. Normalize emails consistently (for example with `Email.downcase(...).strip`) when storing and looking up blocked addresses, and enforce that normalization for existing/admin-created records as well.

findings.title: Concurrent blocked-email checks lose match-count updates
findings.body: `should_block?` reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby, and saves the record. Multiple simultaneous signup attempts for the same blocked address can all read the same value and overwrite one another, so `match_count` and potentially the observed match state are inaccurate. Use an atomic database update such as `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or locking/counter updates.

findings.title: Non-matching blocked-email checks return nil instead of false
findings.body: When no record exists, `record && ...` evaluates to `nil`, not `false`. This contradicts the included `be_false` example for this path (which will fail under RSpec's strict false matcher) and makes the predicate's return type inconsistent. Return an explicit boolean, e.g. `!!record && ...`.
